prize_parts.citation: For a visionary prose and poetic oeuvre in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of rare imaginative scale.

statement.case_for: My opening view stands, and it rests on the common criteria rather than on how many colleagues ranked him first. Public knowledge indicates that Cărtărescu's voice is distinctive: dense, recurrent imagery of the body, memory, dream and cosmology. The Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid appear to give it formal and imaginative ambition on a scale few candidates match. The same imagery seems to recur across poetry, short fiction and the large novels, which supports a citation for the whole oeuvre rather than for one book. The work covers several decades and a late phase that consolidates rather than repeats. Within Nobel's will, this reads as an imaginative and intellectual achievement of real depth. It does not depend on national or political symbolism. I have not read the texts and cannot independently verify them. This judgment rests on general public knowledge and on my colleagues' descriptions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation dependence. The claim concerns dense Romanian sentence rhythm and patterned imagery, and the poetry and early work are unevenly translated, so the committee may be judging the whole corpus from its most visible novels. A second concern is consistency. Very long, recursive, self-enclosed structures may sustain intensity less evenly than the central books suggest, and I cannot verify this from the supplied evidence. If the prose proves to repeat its motifs without deepening them, Adonis has the stronger claim on formal and linguistic renewal of a whole literary language.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first for voice, linguistic achievement and intellectual scope. He warns that Romanian density may be flattened in translation and that the poetry and early fiction are partly inaccessible. He ranks Adonis second and Kincaid third, and he notes that timing is a consideration for Adonis only because of age, which is not a literary criterion.
responses.response: I agree that the central risk is the gap between the Romanian texture and what translation conveys, and I would not claim more than the major novels support. I also agree that Adonis's age is not a literary criterion and should not decide anything. Where I differ is on Kincaid. Her compactness and control are real, but the modest size of the oeuvre limits the case for sustained significance more than it does for Cărtărescu, whose cumulative architecture is the argument. For that reason I keep her outside my top alternatives.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Pierre Michon third, praising his sentence-level density, his concern with vocation and ancestry, and his formal precision. She also acknowledges that the slim corpus weighs on breadth and on the 'greatest benefit' framing.
responses.response: I ranked Michon seventh, and her argument makes me weigh the concentration of his language more seriously than I did. The linguistic achievement looks high. I still hold that a small oeuvre of very high quality is a harder case for a prize based on the whole body of work. The translation risk is also severe, because the effect depends on French syntax and register. I would keep him as a distinguished candidate for later consideration rather than the preferred choice now. I concede that compression is a legitimate form of achievement and not merely a limitation on breadth.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson second. She cites hybrid works that redraw the boundaries between scholarship, lyric, narrative and visual form, and she says they are difficult to compare with novel-centered oeuvres.
responses.response: I ranked Carson fifth, and her comparability point is fair. Common criteria must apply across genres without favoring novels. My hesitation is about citation scope. It is unclear whether the citation should rest on poetry, essay or translation, and some of the strongest works are book-objects whose visual form translation cannot carry. Her formal invention is real, but I find the case for the whole oeuvre less settled than the cases for Cărtărescu, Adonis or Zurita. I could be persuaded if a precise, defensible scope were articulated.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second. He asks whether the lasting poetic achievement outweighs the cultural-critical profile, and he separates the poetry's formal ambition from the public attention to his positions.
responses.response: I agree that the poetry must stay central to any citation and that his public commentary must not substitute for literary assessment. This is why I keep Adonis as my first alternative. Poetry that remakes the language of a major literary tradition is a strong claim, and arguably the strongest on formal and linguistic achievement. The difficulty is that none of us can fully assess prosody and register from translation without Arabic-language expert reports. That uncertainty is larger than for Cărtărescu's prose, and it is the main reason I do not rank Adonis first.

responses.point: Sward ranks Alexis Wright third and Can Xue fourth, praising Wright's polyphonic reshaping of the novel through Indigenous storytelling forms and Can Xue's radical, sustained dream-logic method.
responses.response: Wright's case, in which formal innovation is tied to its subject, is substantial. Since the major novels are few and the oeuvre may still be developing, I cannot judge from the evidence whether this is the right moment. With Can Xue I share Sward's own reservation. It is uncertain whether sustained quality holds across a large body of similar-seeming work, and I lack the Chinese-language input to resolve it. Neither is excluded, but neither has displaced Cărtărescu in my assessment.

uncertainties: I have not read the texts and cannot independently verify any claim. All judgments rest on general public knowledge and on colleagues' descriptions.
Swedish and wider translation coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early fiction is uneven, so the whole-oeuvre claim leans on the major novels.
Whether the late work deepens or repeats the central motifs of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
Assessment of Adonis's prosody and Zurita's verbal texture depends on translation and secondary accounts, and Arabic- and Spanish-language expert assessment is unavailable.
My committee voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, and my simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own non-fiction practice is context, not evidence of preference for any candidate. I was elected to the Academy alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020 and am married to a former finance minister. I see no connection between either fact and any shortlisted writer, and neither requires recusal on the supplied record.
